newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Major urges EU business to fight over-regulation.
newsitem.headline: Major urges EU business to fight over-regulation.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major appealed to businessmen across the European Union on Tuesday to join him in a crusade against over-regulation which he said had cost millions of jobs and threatened many others.

In a hard-hitting speech to about 400 business leaders but aimed at Britain's voters, Major extolled his country's faith in enterprise and the individual, disparaging the "European Social Model" which he said stifled job creation.
"Over-regulation doesn't work, and as a result nor do millions of Europeans," Major said.
"I want the whole of Europe to wake up to the crying need for an enterprise approach so that we can get back to work and we can all prosper."

Implicitly drawing a line between his Conservative Party's views and those of the opposition Labour Party, Major said he would never sign the European Union's Social Chapter, a package of employment laws to which Britain has an opt out.

"One signature on the Social Chapter would mean half a million British signatures on the dole...it would become a Trojan horse unloading on Britain the problems which brought us to a low point in the 1970s," he said.

Major, who praised the "remarkable flexibility" of the United States' labour market, added that the real danger was not so much what was now in the Social Chapter as what could come if Britain joined the other countries in it.
There were, he said, some 18.5 million European Union citizens out of work. British unemployment at around seven percent is well below that in most other major EU countries.
In London, Labour's foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook charged Major with vastly exaggerating the extent of the Social Chapter.

He asked where Major had come up with the "suspiciously round figure" of half a million jobs, and said the real threat to investment in Britain was the civil war in the Conservative Party on EU policy.
Accusing Major of constantly giving way to "Eurosceptics" in his party's ranks, he said: "Our investment and our jobs depend on a successful relationship between Britain and Europe."
Labour, under moderate Tony Blair, leads Major's Conservatives by 16 percentage points in an opinion poll published earlier on Tuesday, with an election due by May 22.
Businessmen attending the Brussels speech generally embraced Major's call for a flexibile employment market.
"What you said is music to the ears," Sygmont Tyszkiewcz, of the European employers federation UNICE, told Major.
EU dignitaries in the audience were less effusive.
Mario Monti, the EU commissioner for the single market, said a rethinking was already going on across the bloc.
Major said measures such as the EU's working time directive which limits the working week to 48 hours were "the thin end of a very large wedge".

"Business needs to speak up and say this. The facts are uncomfortable, but they cannot be ignored. If Europe is heading in the wrong direction...then we must face the problem and change the policy," he said.
